title: M365 Endpoint Administrator
tagline: Deploy, manage, and protect Windows endpoints with Microsoft Intune, Microsoft Entra ID, and Windows Autopilot — scenario-driven prep for the MD-102 Endpoint Administrator.

domains.name: Deploy Windows
domains.summary: Modern Windows deployment with Windows Autopilot, provisioning, and Windows Update for Business servicing.

scenarios.title: Zero-touch for a remote-first rollout
scenarios.situation: Contoso is hiring 400 remote employees across the country. New Windows 11 laptops ship from the OEM directly to each employee's home; IT staff will never physically touch the hardware. The devices must join Microsoft Entra ID, enroll in Intune, and receive the standard app set during first setup.
scenarios.prompt: Which deployment approach meets the requirement with the least IT touch?
evidence: OEM shipment note
The OEM can register device hardware hashes with Contoso's tenant (or IT can import a CSV of hashes) before the devices ship.
Autopilot deployment profile

A user-driven Microsoft Entra join profile is assigned: during out-of-box experience (OOBE) the user signs in with corporate credentials, the device joins Microsoft Entra ID and auto-enrolls in Intune.
OOBE experience
With the profile applied, OOBE is customized (branding, skipped privacy pages) and the Enrollment Status Page tracks app/policy installation before the desktop appears.
choices: Windows Autopilot with imported hardware hashes and a user-driven Microsoft Entra join deployment profile
Lite-touch imaging with the Microsoft Deployment Toolkit at headquarters, then ship each laptop
Email each user a provisioning package (PPKG) to double-click on their personal PC
Reimage every device with WDS multicast at a regional office before shipping
scenarios.why: Windows Autopilot is the cloud-native, zero-touch deployment method: devices ship from the OEM straight to users, and OOBE handles Entra join plus Intune enrollment. MDT/WDS imaging requires IT to touch every device, and a provisioning package on a personal PC does not produce a managed corporate device.
scenarios.hint: Think about which method lets the OEM ship directly to the user's home with no IT hands on the box.
objectives: Describe the Windows Autopilot provisioning flow
Choose a deployment method for remote, no-touch scenarios

scenarios.title: Autopilot devices ignoring the profile
scenarios.situation: Contoso imported 120 hardware hashes into Intune. The devices appear under Devices > Windows > Windows Autopilot devices, but at OOBE users get the generic setup experience instead of the customized Autopilot flow, and devices land in Microsoft Entra ID without the expected device name prefix.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
evidence: Autopilot devices blade
All 120 devices are listed, but the 'Profile status' column shows 'Not assigned'.
Deployment profile assignments
The profile is assigned to the group 'Autopilot-Devices', a dynamic device group.
Dynamic group rule
The group rule filters on device.devicePhysicalIds -any _ -eq "[ZTDID]:<id>" — the ZTDID order ID values captured before the OEM provided the real order IDs.
choices: The deployment profile is not assigned to a group that actually contains the devices, so no profile applies at OOBE
The Enrollment Status Page timeout is too short for the device setup phase
A Windows Update ring policy is conflicting with the Autopilot profile
The devices need a compliance policy before a deployment profile can apply
scenarios.why: Autopilot profiles only apply when assigned to a group containing the Autopilot devices. 'Not assigned' profile status at OOBE means the assignment missed — here the dynamic group rule references stale order IDs, so membership is empty. ESP timeouts, update rings, and compliance policies do not control whether the profile applies.
scenarios.hint: Check the one column in the Autopilot devices list that tells you whether a device picked up its profile.
objectives: Troubleshoot Autopilot profile assignment
Use dynamic groups and profile status to diagnose enrollment issues

scenarios.title: The Enrollment Status Page that never ends
scenarios.situation: Contoso uses Autopilot pre-provisioning: technicians run through the technician flow, then devices ship to users. Recently the technician flow stalls on the Enrollment Status Page during device setup and eventually fails. The ESP is configured with five Win32 apps marked as blocking.
scenarios.prompt: What should the administrator check first?
evidence: ESP configuration
Device setup phase lists 5 blocking apps and 'Show an error when installation takes longer than 60 minutes'.
App install status
Two of the blocking apps report 'Failed' in Intune; their detection rules reference a registry path the new installer version no longer writes.
Intune Management Extension log
IntuneManagementExtension.log shows repeated install retries for the two apps, then ESP device setup times out.
choices: Fix or remove the blocking apps' broken detection rules (or make them non-blocking) so device setup can complete
Rebuild the reference image with the Microsoft Deployment Toolkit
Disable TPM attestation on the devices
Switch the deployment profile from Microsoft Entra join to hybrid Microsoft Entra join
scenarios.why: The ESP device-setup phase waits for every blocking app. Broken detection rules make the Intune Management Extension retry installs until the ESP fails. The fix is at the app layer: correct the detection rules (or demote the apps to non-blocking). Rebuilding images, touching TPM, or changing join type does not address failed app installs.
scenarios.hint: ESP waits for blocking apps — ask what happens when a blocking app can never report success.
objectives: Diagnose Enrollment Status Page failures
Relate app detection rules to ESP blocking behavior

scenarios.title: Pilot Windows 11 24H2 without chaos
scenarios.situation: Contoso runs Windows 11 23H2 on 2,000 Intune-managed devices. The desktop team wants 200 pilot devices on Windows 11 24H2 next month while everyone else stays put, with the ability to pause the rollout if the pilot hits issues.
scenarios.prompt: Which Intune approach implements this most cleanly?
evidence: Windows Update for Business deployment service
Intune manages feature updates through the deployment service: feature update profiles target groups with rollout options including offer dates and deferrals.
Feature update profile settings
A profile can set the feature update to deploy (Windows 11, version 24H2), with rollout options to start on a date, defer a number of days, and pause.
Rings vs profiles
Update rings control how updates install (servicing behavior); feature update profiles control which Windows version is offered. They are separate policy types.
choices: Create a feature updates profile targeting only the pilot group with rollout options (start date, deferral, pause)
Approve the update in WSUS with an aggressive deadline for all devices
Use an expedited quality update policy to push 24H2 to everyone at once
Run Autopilot Reset on the pilot devices so they reinstall on the latest media
scenarios.why: Feature update profiles in Intune, backed by the Windows Update for Business deployment service, target a specific group with a chosen Windows version plus rollout options (schedule, deferral, pause). WSUS deadlines and expedited quality updates do not scope a feature version to a pilot ring; Autopilot Reset reinstalls the OS but is not an update-management strategy.
scenarios.hint: Which Intune policy type picks the Windows version offered to a group — rings, or feature update profiles?
objectives: Use feature update profiles for controlled OS rollouts
Distinguish update rings from feature update profiles

domains.name: Identity and compliance
domains.summary: Microsoft Entra ID device identity, Conditional Access, and device compliance policies.

scenarios.title: Cloud-native join for a cloud-native org
scenarios.situation: Fabrikam has no on-premises Active Directory at all: every workload is in Microsoft 365 and Azure. They are buying 300 new Windows 11 laptops and want single sign-on to Microsoft 365, Intune management, and no on-premises infrastructure.
scenarios.prompt: Which device identity should the administrator choose?
evidence: dsregcmd /status (pilot device)
AzureAdJoined: YES, DomainJoined: NO — the device is joined directly to Microsoft Entra ID.
Infrastructure inventory
No domain controllers, no Microsoft Entra Connect sync server, no AD DS forest exist in the environment.
SSO behavior
Users sign in with their Microsoft Entra credentials and get SSO to Microsoft 365 apps with no on-premises dependency.
choices: Microsoft Entra joined
Microsoft Entra hybrid joined
Microsoft Entra registered (workplace join)
Workgroup with manual Intune enrollment and no Entra identity
scenarios.why: Microsoft Entra joined is the cloud-native identity: devices join the cloud directory directly with no AD DS or sync infrastructure. Hybrid join requires on-premises AD plus Microsoft Entra Connect sync; Entra registered is a BYOD-level identity without full management; workgroup gives up Entra identity and SSO entirely.
scenarios.hint: Hybrid join needs something on-premises. Fabrikam has nothing on-premises — what does that leave?
objectives: Compare Entra joined, hybrid joined, and registered
Select a device identity for a cloud-only organization

scenarios.title: Why is everyone blocked from SharePoint?
scenarios.situation: After migrating the last laptops from hybrid join to Microsoft Entra joined, users report being blocked from SharePoint Online and Teams. The Conditional Access sign-in logs show the failure on a policy named 'Require corporate device'. Devices are compliant in Intune.
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause and the correct fix?
evidence: CA policy grant controls
'Require corporate device' uses the grant control 'Require hybrid Microsoft Entra joined device'.
Sign-in log (blocked event)
Device info: Trust type = Microsoft Entra joined; Join type does not satisfy the hybrid-join grant control.
Intune device state
Devices show Compliant = Yes in Intune; compliance is healthy.
choices: Change the grant control to 'Require device to be marked as compliant' since the fleet is now Entra joined and compliant
Rejoin all devices as hybrid joined to satisfy the old policy
Disable the Conditional Access policy entirely
Mark the devices as compliant manually in Microsoft Entra ID
scenarios.why: The policy's grant control requires hybrid join, which no longer matches the fleet after the cloud migration — even though devices are compliant. The correct fix is to update the grant control to 'require device to be marked as compliant', which reflects the current healthy state. Reverting the migration, disabling the policy, or manual marking are wrong or unsupported.
scenarios.hint: The devices are compliant but the policy asks for something else — what exactly does the grant control demand?
objectives: Interpret Conditional Access sign-in logs
Align grant controls with the actual device identity after migration

scenarios.title: MFA everywhere except the break-glass account
scenarios.situation: Contoso's security team requires multifactor authentication for all users via Conditional Access. They also maintain two emergency-access (break-glass) accounts that must be able to sign in during an outage of the MFA provider.
scenarios.prompt: How should the administrator configure this?
evidence: CA policy user assignment
The 'Require MFA for all users' policy targets 'All users' with no exclusions; the break-glass accounts are currently included.
Microsoft guidance

Emergency access accounts should be excluded from Conditional Access policies (and from MFA requirements) so they remain usable during identity outages, while being monitored and secured with long, stored credentials.
Grant controls
The policy grants access only if MFA is completed.
choices: Exclude the emergency-access accounts from the MFA policy and monitor their use
Disable the Conditional Access policy during the next maintenance window
Rely on per-user MFA state instead of Conditional Access
Add a second grant control requiring an approved client app for the break-glass accounts
scenarios.why: Best practice is to exclude emergency-access accounts from Conditional Access MFA policies so they stay available during an MFA/identity outage, compensating with strong stored credentials and alerting. Disabling the policy or using per-user MFA weakens the posture; adding more grant controls to break-glass accounts defeats their purpose.
scenarios.hint: Break-glass accounts exist for the day MFA itself is down — what must be true of them on that day?
objectives: Design Conditional Access exclusions safely
Apply emergency-access account best practices

scenarios.title: BitLocker: configured but not compliant
scenarios.situation: Contoso enables BitLocker through a settings catalog profile, and most devices report the setting applied. But the compliance dashboard shows dozens of devices 'Not compliant' for encryption, and Conditional Access blocks those devices from Exchange Online because the policy requires compliant devices.
evidence: Settings catalog report
The BitLocker settings show 'Succeeded' on the affected devices.
Compliance policy
No device compliance policy exists that includes an encryption rule; only the configuration profile was deployed.
Conditional Access
The Exchange Online policy grants access only to devices marked compliant.
choices: Create a device compliance policy with an encryption rule and an action for noncompliance, so encryption state is evaluated and enforced
Re-push the settings catalog profile with a higher priority
Enable co-management and move the compliance workload to Configuration Manager
Wipe the noncompliant devices so they re-encrypt
scenarios.why: Configuration profiles set device state; compliance policies evaluate state against rules and produce the compliant/noncompliant verdict that Conditional Access consumes. Without a compliance policy containing an encryption rule, Intune never evaluates BitLocker, so devices stay noncompliant (or unevaluated) and CA blocks them. Re-pushing the profile does not create the evaluation.
scenarios.hint: Settings say 'what should be'. Which policy type decides 'is it compliant, and what happens if not'?
objectives: Distinguish compliance policies from configuration profiles
Connect compliance state to Conditional Access decisions

domains.name: Device management and endpoint security
domains.summary: Intune configuration profiles, endpoint security baselines, Defender for Endpoint, and remote actions.

scenarios.title: Baseline or settings catalog?
scenarios.situation: The CISO wants Microsoft's recommended security posture — Defender antivirus, BitLocker, firewall, attack surface reduction — applied to 2,000 Windows devices quickly and kept aligned with Microsoft's best practices as they evolve.
scenarios.prompt: Which Intune tool is the best fit for the initial rollout?
evidence: Security baselines

Endpoint security > Security baselines ships curated setting groups (e.g., MDM Security Baseline for Windows, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Baseline) representing Microsoft's recommended configuration.
Settings catalog
Offers thousands of individual settings for fine-grained custom configuration, but every value must be chosen and maintained manually.
Compliance policy
Evaluates whether settings are in the desired state; it does not configure the settings themselves.
choices: Deploy the MDM Security Baseline to establish Microsoft's recommended posture, then customize with the settings catalog only where needed
Build every setting by hand in the settings catalog from a blank profile
Deploy a compliance policy and let it configure the settings
Configure the settings with Group Policy instead of Intune
scenarios.why: Security baselines are purpose-built for this: Microsoft-curated, recommended settings in one deployable package. The settings catalog is the right tool for custom, granular needs, but starting from scratch duplicates the baseline's work. Compliance policies evaluate state rather than configure it, and Group Policy moves backward from cloud-native management.
scenarios.hint: Which option ships with Microsoft's recommendations already filled in?
objectives: Choose between security baselines and the settings catalog
Apply Microsoft-recommended endpoint posture efficiently

scenarios.title: The right remote action for a departing contractor
scenarios.situation: A contractor returns a corporate-owned laptop that must be sanitized and redeployed to the next hire. Separately, a former employee's personal phone (BYOD) still has the Outlook app with corporate mail; IT must remove company data without touching personal photos.
scenarios.prompt: Which pair of Intune remote actions is correct?
evidence: Wipe
Factory-resets the device, removing all data, apps, and settings. Options exist to retain enrollment state for Autopilot re-provisioning.
Retire
Removes company data and unenrolls the device from Intune. On BYOD devices this performs a selective wipe that leaves personal data intact.
Ownership
The laptop is corporate-owned; the phone is personally owned (BYOD).
choices: Wipe the corporate laptop; Retire the BYOD phone
Wipe both devices
Retire both devices
Run Autopilot Reset on the phone and Wipe on the laptop
scenarios.why: Wipe is the full factory reset appropriate for a corporate device being redeployed. Retire is the selective, company-data-only removal designed for BYOD — it unenrolls and removes corporate data while preserving personal content. Wiping the personal phone would destroy personal data; retiring the laptop would not sanitize it for the next user.
scenarios.hint: Match the blast radius of the action to the ownership of the device.
objectives: Select the correct Intune remote action by scenario
Protect personal data on BYOD during offboarding

scenarios.title: Moving Endpoint Protection to Intune
scenarios.situation: Contoso is co-managed: Configuration Manager and Intune both manage the Windows fleet. Leadership wants Intune to become the authority for antivirus, firewall, and encryption policy while Configuration Manager keeps handling OS imaging for now.
scenarios.prompt: Where does the administrator make this change?
evidence: Co-management workloads

In the Configuration Manager console, co-management properties include a Workloads tab with sliders for: Compliance policies, Device configuration, Endpoint Protection, Resource access policies, Client apps, Office Click-to-Run apps, and Windows Update policies.
Workload states
Each workload can be set to Configuration Manager, Pilot Intune, or Intune.
Current state
All workloads currently sit with Configuration Manager.
choices: In Configuration Manager co-management properties, move the Endpoint Protection workload slider to Pilot Intune (then Intune)
Delete the Configuration Manager antivirus policies and hope Intune takes over
Uninstall the Configuration Manager client from all devices
Create an Intune compliance policy named 'Endpoint Protection'
scenarios.why: Co-management authority is decided per workload in Configuration Manager's co-management properties. Moving the Endpoint Protection slider to Pilot Intune (for a pilot collection) and then to Intune hands that authority to Intune while leaving imaging with Configuration Manager. Deleting policies or uninstalling the client is destructive and uncontrolled; a compliance policy does not own endpoint protection settings.
scenarios.hint: Co-management has a specific blade where each workload's authority is chosen — which workload, and which direction?
objectives: Manage co-management workload authority
Transition endpoint protection to Intune in phases

scenarios.title: Attack surface reduction vs. the line-of-business app
scenarios.situation: Contoso enforces the ASR rule 'Block Office applications from creating child processes'. The finance team's macro-driven reporting tool (a legitimate LOB app launched from Excel) is now blocked, and month-end close is at risk.
evidence: ASR rule modes
ASR rules support Audit, Block, Warn, and Disable modes; Microsoft recommends running new rules in Audit mode first to measure impact.
Exclusions
Endpoint security policies support exclusions for specific files, folders, and processes so a known-good app can be exempted without weakening the rule elsewhere.
Incident scope
Only the finance reporting tool is affected; no malware alerts are associated with the blocks.
choices: Add a scoped exclusion for the finance app in the ASR policy (and use Audit mode when rolling out new rules)
Disable Microsoft Defender Antivirus on the finance team's devices
Exclude the entire C: drive from the ASR rule
Disable the ASR rule tenant-wide permanently
scenarios.why: The safe pattern is audit-first, then narrowly scoped exclusions for the known-good application — the rule keeps protecting everything else. Disabling Defender, excluding whole drives, or killing the rule tenant-wide trades a targeted business exception for a broad security hole.
scenarios.hint: The rule is doing its job everywhere except one known-good app — how do you carve out just that app?
objectives: Tune attack surface reduction rules safely
Use audit mode and exclusions for business exceptions

domains.name: Manage applications
domains.summary: App deployment with Intune: Win32 apps, Microsoft Store apps, and app protection policies.

scenarios.title: Packaging the Win32 app
scenarios.situation: Contoso must deploy a vendor monitoring agent (setup.exe with silent switches) to 500 Windows devices via Intune, targeting it as required so it installs without user interaction.
scenarios.prompt: What preparation does Intune require before the app can be deployed?
evidence: Win32 app management
Intune deploys Win32 apps as .intunewin packages created by the Microsoft Win32 Content Prep Tool (IntuneWinAppUtil.exe).
App definition
The admin provides install and uninstall command lines plus detection rules (MSI product code, file/registry existence, version checks) so Intune knows when the app is present.
Delivery
Required Win32 apps install via the Intune Management Extension without user interaction.
choices: Convert setup.exe to .intunewin with IntuneWinAppUtil.exe, then define install/uninstall commands and detection rules
Upload setup.exe directly to Intune as a line-of-business app
Repackage the agent as an MSIX before Intune will accept it
Email the installer link to users and mark the app as available
scenarios.why: Win32 deployment in Intune requires the .intunewin format produced by IntuneWinAppUtil.exe, plus install/uninstall commands and detection rules that let the agent detect success. Raw setup.exe uploads are not a Win32 app type, MSIX repackaging is unnecessary, and an emailed link is not managed deployment.
scenarios.hint: Which Microsoft tool converts a setup.exe into the format Intune's Win32 app type expects?
objectives: Package Win32 apps with the Content Prep Tool
Define detection rules for reliable app state

scenarios.title: Required app never installs on 30 devices
scenarios.situation: A required Win32 app installed cleanly on 470 of 500 devices. On the remaining 30 — online, synced, and otherwise healthy — Intune reports the app as 'Not installed' and never retries. Other required apps install fine on those same devices.
scenarios.prompt: What should the administrator investigate first?
evidence: IntuneManagementExtension.log (affected device)
Shows the app evaluated as 'not applicable / already detected' and skipped — the agent believes the detection rule is already satisfied.
Detection rule
The rule checks for a registry value under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Vendor\Agent that the newest installer writes to a different path.
Assignment
The app is assigned as Required to the same group containing all 500 devices.
choices: The detection rule is misconfigured, so Intune thinks the app is already installed and skips it
Reassign the app as Available instead of Required
Wipe the 30 devices and let them re-enroll
Extend the Enrollment Status Page timeout
scenarios.why: When the agent believes the detection rule is satisfied, it skips installation without error — the classic symptom of a wrong registry path or version check. Assignment, enrollment health, and ESP timeouts are ruled out because the devices are healthy and other required apps install. Fix the detection rule to match what the installer actually writes.
scenarios.hint: Intune skips the install without an error — what component decides 'already installed'?
objectives: Troubleshoot Win32 app detection rules
Read Intune Management Extension behavior from symptoms

scenarios.title: Protecting Outlook data on personal phones
scenarios.situation: Contoso allows BYOD but will not enroll personal phones in MDM. Security still requires: a PIN to open Outlook and Teams, encryption of corporate data inside those apps, and blocking copy/paste from corporate content into personal apps.
scenarios.prompt: Which Intune mechanism delivers this without device enrollment?
evidence: App protection policies (MAM)
Protect corporate data inside managed apps without enrolling the device. They target apps that integrate the Intune SDK / App SDK (Outlook, Teams, OneDrive, Edge).
Policy settings
Require PIN for access, encrypt app data, and restrict cut/copy/paste and 'open in' to managed apps only.
Enrollment requirement
App protection policies can apply to devices that are only Microsoft Entra registered, with no MDM enrollment.
choices: App protection policies targeting Outlook and Teams
Device compliance policies requiring encryption
A Conditional Access policy blocking all mobile access
A device configuration profile with an Exchange ActiveSync payload
scenarios.why: App protection policies (mobile application management) secure data at the app layer without MDM enrollment — exactly the BYOD requirement. Compliance policies and configuration profiles need enrollment; blocking mobile access in CA prevents work rather than protecting it.
scenarios.hint: Which policy type protects data inside the app when the device itself is unmanaged?
objectives: Apply app protection policies for unenrolled BYOD
Choose MAM vs MDM for data protection

scenarios.title: Superseding the old VPN client
scenarios.situation: Contoso is replacing VPN client v1 with v2. When v2 installs, v1 must be cleanly uninstalled so the two drivers never coexist. Both are deployed as Win32 apps in Intune.
scenarios.prompt: Which Intune feature implements the replacement?
evidence: Supersedence
A Win32 app can declare a supersedence relationship to an older app, with the option to uninstall the previous version when the new one installs.
Dependencies
Dependencies control install order (install B before A), not replacement.
Assignment types
Required / Available / Uninstall control targeting, not version replacement.
choices: Configure a supersedence relationship on the v2 app pointing to v1, set to uninstall the previous version
Assign v2 as Required and v1 as Uninstall to the same group and hope the timing works
Add v1 as a dependency of v2
Delete the v1 app from Intune
scenarios.why: Supersedence is the purpose-built mechanism: v2 supersedes v1 and Intune uninstalls v1 as part of installing v2, in the right order. Parallel Required/Uninstall assignments race; dependencies enforce order without removing the old app; deleting v1 from Intune does not uninstall it from devices.
scenarios.hint: Intune has a relationship type specifically for 'new version replaces old' — what is it called?
objectives: Use supersedence for app version replacement
Distinguish supersedence from dependencies and assignments

lessons.title: Deploying Windows the modern way
concepts: Windows Autopilot is Microsoft's cloud-native provisioning technology: instead of building and maintaining custom OS images, IT registers each device's hardware hash in Intune and the device configures itself during the out-of-box experience (OOBE). Devices can ship from the OEM or reseller directly to the user, which is what makes zero-touch deployment possible.

The hardware hash uniquely identifies the device to the Autopilot service. IT collects it with the Get-WindowsAutopilotInfo script (or receives a CSV from the OEM), imports it under Windows Autopilot devices, and assigns a deployment profile. Until a profile is assigned, the device shows 'Not assigned' and OOBE runs the generic flow.

Autopilot deployment profiles come in two main modes. User-driven mode prompts the user to sign in with corporate credentials and is the standard choice for primary-user devices. Self-deploying mode provisions without any user interaction and is designed for shared devices, kiosks, and digital signage.

The Enrollment Status Page (ESP) controls what the user sees while policies and apps install. It has a device setup phase (runs before the user signs in, used by pre-provisioning flows where a technician prepares the device) and an account setup phase. Apps marked as blocking must install successfully before the phase completes, which is why broken detection rules on blocking apps stall the ESP.

For devices that cannot use Autopilot, dynamic provisioning uses provisioning packages (PPKG files) built with Windows Configuration Designer to apply settings, join Entra ID, enroll in Intune, and install apps from a USB drive or network share.

Windows servicing is managed through the Windows Update for Business deployment service in Intune. Update rings control servicing behavior (how and when updates install), while feature update profiles control which Windows version is offered, with rollout options for start dates, deferrals, pauses, and expedited installation. Quality updates (including expedite policies for urgent patches) and driver updates are managed as separate policy types.

example.code:
# Collect the hardware hash and upload it to Intune (Autopilot registration)
Install-Script -Name Get-WindowsAutopilotInfo -Force
Get-WindowsAutopilotInfo.ps1 -Online

# Verify the device landed in Autopilot and check its profile status
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "DeviceManagementServiceConfig.Read.All"
Get-MgDeviceManagementWindowsAutopilotDeviceIdentity | 
    Select-Object SerialNumber, Manufacturer, Model, DeploymentProfileAssignmentStatus
example.walkthrough: The first two lines install Microsoft's Get-WindowsAutopilotInfo script and run it with -Online, which captures the device's hardware hash and uploads it directly to the tenant's Autopilot device list. The second block connects to Microsoft Graph and lists Autopilot device identities with their deployment-profile assignment status — the same 'Not assigned' vs 'Assigned' state you see in the Intune admin center — so you can confirm the profile will apply before the device reaches OOBE.

pitfalls: Importing hardware hashes but never assigning a deployment profile: devices enroll with the generic OOBE and miss naming templates, ESP config, and app targeting.
Dynamic group rules for Autopilot assignment that reference stale order IDs (ZTDID) or wrong purchase order values, leaving the assignment group empty.
Marking Win32 apps as blocking in the ESP when their detection rules are untested — one broken rule stalls every pre-provisioned device.
Confusing update rings with feature update profiles: rings govern install behavior, profiles govern which Windows version is offered. You need the right one for version targeting.
Hybrid Autopilot deployments require the Intune Connector for Active Directory on-premises; forgetting it breaks hybrid join during OOBE.
lessons.try_it: In a trial tenant, create a user-driven Microsoft Entra join Autopilot deployment profile with a device naming template (e.g., CTX-%SERIAL%). List which apps you would mark as blocking vs non-blocking in the ESP, and write one sentence justifying each choice.

lessons.title: Identity and access: Entra ID, Conditional Access, compliance
concepts: Every managed Windows device carries a Microsoft Entra device identity. Microsoft Entra joined means the device joins the cloud directory directly — the cloud-native choice with no on-premises infrastructure. Microsoft Entra hybrid joined means the device is joined to on-premises Active Directory and synchronized to the cloud via Microsoft Entra Connect. Microsoft Entra registered (workplace join) is the lightweight BYOD identity that enables SSO without full management.

Conditional Access is the policy engine that decides, per sign-in, whether access is granted. Every policy has assignments (which users, cloud apps, and conditions trigger it), access controls (grant: require MFA, require compliant device, require hybrid joined device, block; session: sign-in frequency, app-enforced restrictions), and an enablement state. Policies are evaluated together — the most restrictive applicable outcome wins.

The signals Conditional Access evaluates include user and group membership, device platform, location (named locations), client app type, device state (compliant, hybrid joined), and risk (user risk and sign-in risk from Identity Protection). A policy that requires 'hybrid joined device' will block a fleet that has moved to Entra joined, even when every device is compliant.

Device compliance policies define the rules a device must satisfy: OS version, encryption (BitLocker), password complexity, antivirus status, and more. Actions for noncompliance escalate on a schedule — mark the device noncompliant, send email to the user, or remotely lock — and the resulting compliance state is what Conditional Access grant controls like 'require device to be marked as compliant' consume.

Configuration profiles and compliance policies are complementary, not interchangeable. Configuration profiles (settings catalog, templates) push the desired state to the device; compliance policies measure whether the device meets the rules and drive access decisions. Deploying BitLocker settings without a compliance policy leaves Conditional Access blind to encryption state.

Emergency-access (break-glass) accounts are excluded from Conditional Access MFA policies by design, so administrators can recover the tenant during an identity outage. They are secured with long, randomly generated credentials stored offline and monitored with alerts on any sign-in.

example.code:
# List Conditional Access policies and their grant controls
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "Policy.Read.All"
Get-MgIdentityConditionalAccessPolicy | 
    Select-Object DisplayName, State,
        @{n="GrantControls";e={$_.GrantControls.BuiltInControls -join ", "}}

# Check a device's join and compliance state (the signals CA evaluates)
dsregcmd /status | Select-String "AzureAdJoined|DomainJoined|EnterpriseJoined"
example.walkthrough: The first block connects to Microsoft Graph and enumerates every Conditional Access policy with its state and built-in grant controls — the fastest way to spot a stale 'require hybrid joined device' control after a cloud migration. The second command runs dsregcmd /status on a Windows device and filters for the join-state lines, showing exactly the device-identity signals (Entra joined vs domain joined) that Conditional Access sees during evaluation.

pitfalls: Requiring hybrid-joined devices in Conditional Access after migrating the fleet to Entra joined — mass blocks despite healthy compliance.
Forgetting to exclude emergency-access accounts from CA policies, which can lock out recovery during an MFA outage.
Assuming a configuration profile alone makes devices 'compliant' — without a compliance policy, Conditional Access has no verdict to consume.
Blocking legacy authentication without an inventory of what still uses it (old mail clients, LOB apps) — plan the block with report-only mode and sign-in logs first.
Compliance state refreshes on the device check-in cycle, not instantly — allow time after remediating before re-testing access.
lessons.try_it: Open the Conditional Access 'What If' tool in a trial tenant and evaluate a test user accessing SharePoint from a noncompliant device. Record which policy applies and which grant control fires, then change the device state to compliant and re-run.

lessons.title: Protecting endpoints with Intune
concepts: Intune configures devices with configuration profiles. The settings catalog exposes thousands of individual settings for fine-grained control, while templates package common scenarios (Endpoint protection, Device restrictions, Wi-Fi, VPN). Profiles target devices or users, and assignment filters can narrow targeting further — for example, applying a profile only to devices with a specific OS version.

Endpoint security baselines are Microsoft's curated starting point: the MDM Security Baseline and the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Baseline bundle recommended settings for Defender, BitLocker, firewalls, and attack surface reduction. Deploy a baseline for the recommended posture first, then layer settings-catalog customizations only where the organization differs.

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint onboarding can be driven from Intune's endpoint security blade: devices onboard to Defender for Endpoint, which adds endpoint detection and response (EDR), threat and vulnerability management, and the device timeline. The Intune connector for Defender for Endpoint also enables security tasks — remediation actions pushed from the Defender portal to Intune-managed devices.

Attack surface reduction (ASR) rules harden the OS against common attack techniques, such as Office apps spawning child processes or executables running from email clients. Each rule supports Audit, Block, Warn, and Disable modes — Microsoft's recommended rollout is audit-first to measure business impact, then enforce with narrowly scoped exclusions for legitimate apps.

Intune remote actions map to lifecycle events. Retire removes corporate data and unenrolls (selective wipe on BYOD, preserving personal content). Wipe factory-resets the device for redeployment, with an option to retain enrollment state. Fresh Start removes preinstalled OEM apps while keeping user data. Autopilot Reset strips apps and settings while keeping the Autopilot enrollment. Remote lock, restart, sync, locate, and collect-diagnostics cover day-to-day support.

Co-management lets Configuration Manager and Intune share authority over a device, decided per workload: compliance policies, device configuration, endpoint protection, resource access, client apps, Office apps, and Windows Update policies each have a slider set to Configuration Manager, Pilot Intune, or Intune. Move workloads one at a time, piloting each before flipping the fleet.

example.code:
# Inventory managed devices: join-relevant fields Intune reports
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All"
Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -Filter "operatingSystem eq 'Windows'" | 
    Select-Object DeviceName, ManagedDeviceOwnerType, ComplianceState,
        ManagementState, LastSyncDateTime | Format-Table -AutoSize

# Local truth: is this device Entra joined and healthy?
dsregcmd /status
example.walkthrough: The Graph query lists Windows devices Intune manages with the fields that matter for protection decisions: ownership type (corporate vs personal, which drives Retire-vs-Wipe choices), compliance state (what Conditional Access consumes), and last sync time (whether policy is current). dsregcmd /status gives the on-device counterpart — the join and SSO state — so you can correlate what Intune believes with what the device reports when troubleshooting.

pitfalls: Using Retire on a corporate device being redeployed (leaves user data behind) or Wipe on a BYOD phone (destroys personal data) — match the action to ownership.
Deploying ASR rules straight to Block without an audit phase, then firefighting blocked line-of-business apps during month-end close.
Treating a security baseline as a one-time push: baselines evolve, and new baseline versions should be reviewed and adopted deliberately.
Flipping every co-management workload to Intune at once instead of piloting one workload at a time.
Assuming Fresh Start is available everywhere — it is not supported on all device types and scenarios, so verify before promising it in runbooks.
lessons.try_it: Write a one-page runbook for a lost corporate laptop: list the Intune remote actions in order (locate, remote lock, collect diagnostics, wipe) and note at which point you would involve the security team for a Defender for Endpoint investigation.

lessons.title: Deploying and protecting apps
concepts: Intune supports several app types for Windows. Win32 apps (packaged as .intunewin with the Microsoft Win32 Content Prep Tool) handle traditional setup.exe/MSI installers with full install logic. Line-of-business MSI apps cover simple MSI installs. Microsoft Store apps (the new Store, backed by the public winget repository) deploy modern packaged apps, and Microsoft 365 apps are deployed through the dedicated Microsoft 365 apps admin flow.

Every Win32 app definition needs install and uninstall command lines and detection rules — MSI product codes, file existence, or registry keys — that tell the Intune Management Extension whether the app is present. Wrong detection rules are the number-one cause of 'not installed' mysteries: the agent believes the app is already there and skips it silently.

Relationships between apps are explicit. Dependencies force install order (install the runtime before the app). Supersedence declares replacement: the new app version can uninstall the old one during install, which is how you guarantee two VPN client drivers never coexist.

Assignments express intent: Required installs automatically (Win32 required apps install via the Management Extension without user interaction), Available for enrolled devices publishes to Company Portal for self-service, and Uninstall removes. Delivery Optimization and update rings keep the network impact of large required deployments under control.

App protection policies (mobile application management) secure corporate data inside apps without enrolling the device. Targeted at Intune SDK-integrated apps like Outlook, Teams, and OneDrive, they enforce PIN on launch, encrypt app data, and restrict cut/copy/paste and 'open in' to managed apps — the standard answer for BYOD where MDM enrollment is off the table.

App configuration policies push settings into managed apps (for example, preconfiguring the Outlook profile or Teams meeting defaults), and they work both for enrolled devices and for managed apps under app protection policies. Managed app logs can be collected from the Company Portal for troubleshooting.

example.code:
# Package a Win32 app for Intune (Microsoft Win32 Content Prep Tool)
.\IntuneWinAppUtil.exe -c .\Source -s setup.exe -o .\Output

# Verify what the package contains before uploading
Get-ChildItem .\Output -Filter *.intunewin | 
    Select-Object Name, Length, LastWriteTime

# After upload, confirm the app object exists in Intune
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "DeviceManagementApps.Read.All"
Get-MgDeviceAppManagementMobileApp -Filter "displayName eq 'Contoso Agent'" | 
    Select-Object DisplayName, Publisher, @{n="Type";e={$_.ODataType}}
example.walkthrough: IntuneWinAppUtil.exe with -c (source folder), -s (setup file), and -o (output folder) converts the vendor installer into the .intunewin package Intune's Win32 app type requires. The listing step confirms the package was produced; the Graph query then verifies the uploaded app object exists in Intune with its publisher and type. After this, the remaining work happens in the Intune admin center: install/uninstall commands, detection rules, dependencies or supersedence, and assignment.

pitfalls: Detection rules that check a path the installer does not actually write — the app installs once, is never detected, and Intune retries forever (or skips silently if the rule wrongly matches).
Forgetting uninstall command lines on Win32 apps, which makes later supersedence and clean removal impossible.
Assuming app protection policies work on any app — they require apps integrated with the Intune App SDK (the Microsoft 365 mobile apps are the canonical set).
Deploying the new Microsoft Store apps while legacy Store-for-Business assumptions linger: the new Store flow is winget-backed with different licensing behavior.
Assigning a large Win32 app as Required to thousands of devices on day one without Delivery Optimization or phased rollout, saturating branch links.
lessons.try_it: Pick a real utility with a silent installer (e.g., a PDF reader). Write its install command line, uninstall command line, and two detection rules (file-based and registry-based). Then describe when you would use supersedence vs a plain Uninstall assignment to replace it.

labs.title: Trace a Conditional Access block to its policy
labs.objective: Given a blocked sign-in, use Microsoft Graph and on-device state to identify the failing Conditional Access grant control and propose the fix.
steps: Connect to Microsoft Graph with the policy read scope: Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "Policy.Read.All".
List Conditional Access policies and note each policy's state and built-in grant controls.
Identify the policy whose grant control (e.g., 'Require hybrid Microsoft Entra joined device') cannot be satisfied by an Entra joined, compliant fleet.
On a sample device, run dsregcmd /status and confirm the AzureAdJoined / DomainJoined values match the sign-in log's trust type.
Propose the corrected grant control ('Require device to be marked as compliant') and describe how you would validate with the What If tool before enabling.

checks.hint: Enumerate Conditional Access policies with Get-MgIdentityConditionalAccessPolicy and inspect displayName and grant controls.
Run dsregcmd /status on the device and look for the AzureAdJoined line to confirm its join type.

labs.title: Package and validate a Win32 app
labs.objective: Convert a setup.exe into an .intunewin package, define detection rules, and verify the app object in Intune via Microsoft Graph.
steps: Stage the vendor installer in a source folder (e.g., .\Source\setup.exe) and note its silent install switches.
Run the Microsoft Win32 Content Prep Tool: .\IntuneWinAppUtil.exe -c .\Source -s setup.exe -o .\Output.
Confirm the .intunewin package exists in the output folder.
Write the install command line, the uninstall command line, and one registry-based detection rule for the app.
After uploading in the Intune admin center, query Microsoft Graph for the mobile app object and confirm its display name and publisher.

checks.hint: Run IntuneWinAppUtil.exe with -c (source), -s (setup file), and -o (output) to produce the .intunewin package.
Query the uploaded app with Get-MgDeviceAppManagementMobileApp and check displayName.

sections.heading: Intune policy types
items: Configuration profiles (settings catalog, templates) push desired state to devices; they do not judge compliance.
Compliance policies define rules (encryption, OS version, password) and actions for noncompliance; Conditional Access consumes the verdict.
Endpoint security baselines (MDM Security Baseline, Defender for Endpoint Baseline) deploy Microsoft's recommended security posture as a starting point.
Update rings control servicing behavior; feature update profiles control which Windows version is offered; quality/driver/expedite policies are separate types.
App protection policies (MAM) secure data inside apps without device enrollment; app configuration policies push app settings.

sections.heading: Microsoft Entra ID join types
items: Microsoft Entra joined: cloud-native join, no on-premises AD required; full SSO and Intune management.
Microsoft Entra hybrid joined: joined to on-premises AD and synced via Microsoft Entra Connect; needs the Intune Connector for Autopilot hybrid flows.
Microsoft Entra registered: lightweight workplace join for BYOD; SSO without full management.
Check join state on-device with dsregcmd /status (AzureAdJoined, DomainJoined).

sections.heading: Conditional Access components
items: Assignments: users/groups, cloud apps, and conditions that trigger the policy; exclude emergency-access accounts.
Signals (conditions): device platform, locations, client apps, device state, user/sign-in risk.
Grant controls: require MFA, require compliant device, require hybrid joined device, require approved client app, block access.
Session controls: sign-in frequency, persistent browser session, app-enforced restrictions, Conditional Access App Control.
Troubleshoot with sign-in logs and the What If tool; test in report-only mode before enforcing.

sections.heading: Intune remote actions
items: Retire: removes company data and unenrolls; selective wipe on BYOD preserves personal data.
Wipe: factory reset for redeployment; option to retain enrollment state for Autopilot.
Fresh Start: removes preinstalled OEM apps, keeps user data (not available on all device types).
Autopilot Reset: strips apps/settings while keeping Autopilot enrollment.
Day-to-day: sync, restart, remote lock, locate device, collect diagnostics.
